title: Why classes?
learningGoals: see why parallel lists are fragile
meet the idea of bundling data and actions

youtube.title: Python Classes: Why We Need Them (Beginner) | Python Programming EP 61
youtube.description: In this episode you will see why parallel lists are fragile, meet the idea of bundling data and actions and read a first tiny class, with Xecxec the crab. 0:00 Intro · 0:15 One thing, one bundle · 1:00 Parallel lists · 1:40 Two cupboards, one student · 2:13 Second program · 3:13 Recap · 3:44 Bug of the Day · 4:32 Challenge · 4:52 Next episode

scenes.narration: Until now, one student meant a name in one list and marks in another. Today we bundle them together.

scenes.onScreen: "One thing, one bundle": three numbered lines (1. Data about one thing belongs together; 2. A class is a blueprint for such a bundle; 3. An object is one real bundle made from it) and an analogy card: a student file: the name, the marks and the class all live in one folder, not in three different cupboards
scenes.animation: Lines spring in one by one with a pop; the analogy card slides in from the right
scenes.narration: Imagine you track students. One list holds the names. Another list holds the marks. They line up only by position. Move one item, and everything goes wrong. A class fixes this. It is a blueprint for one type of thing. It says what data each thing carries, and what it can do. An object is one real thing built from the blueprint. Think of a student file. Name, marks and class live in one folder, so they can never get separated.

code.source:
names = ["Asha", "Ravi", "Meera"]
marks = [91, 78, 85]
for i in range(len(names)):
    print(names[i], marks[i])
best = marks.index(max(marks))
print("Top:", names[best])

scenes.onScreen: A student whose name is in cupboard one and marks in cupboard two, then a single folder holding both
scenes.animation: Two cupboards with labelled drawers, an arrow pairs them by position, then both drawers merge into one folder
scenes.narration: Here is the problem. The name of Asha sits in one cupboard. Her marks sit in another. If you sort one cupboard, or delete from one, the match breaks, and Asha gets Ravi's marks. A class puts both into one folder. When you move the folder, everything inside moves together. That is the whole idea of bundling.

lines: The name of Asha sits in one cupboard.

scenes.animation: Second program or a twist on the first; [HL n] and [TRACK name=value] cues drive the variable tracker; output panel fills line by line with a ding per line
scenes.narration: [HL 1] The word class starts a blueprint. The name is Student, with a capital letter. [HL 2] Pass means, nothing inside yet. [HL 4] Student with brackets builds one object, tied to a. [HL 5] We give it a name. [HL 6] And marks. [HL 7] A second student, tied to b. [HL 8] With its own name. [HL 9] And its own marks. [HL 10] Each object keeps its own data. Asha ninety one. [HL 11] Ravi seventy eight. Next episodes make this tidier.

code.source:
class Student:
    pass

a = Student()
a.name = "Asha"
a.marks = 91
b = Student()
b.name = "Ravi"
b.marks = 78
print(a.name, a.marks)
print(b.name, b.marks)

scenes.onScreen: BUG OF THE DAY: parallel lists out of sync
scenes.animation: Butter banner drops in with a buzzer; wrong code shakes; the Python error lines appear in tomato; the fix slides in and the terminal turns mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Bug of the Day. We sort only the names. The marks stay where they were. Now Ravi is shown with ninety one, which belongs to Asha. No error appears. You get only wrong answers. That is the worst type of bug. Keep each name and its marks together in one bundle, and they can never drift apart.

props.wrongCode:
names = ["Asha", "Ravi", "Meera"]
marks = [91, 78, 85]
names.sort(reverse=True)
for i in range(len(names)):
    print(names[i], marks[i])
props.fixedCode:
students = [("Asha", 91), ("Ravi", 78), ("Meera", 85)]
students.sort(reverse=True)
for name, mark in students:
    print(name, mark)
props.why: Sorting one list moved the names but not the marks, so the pairs broke. Keeping each name and mark together in one bundle makes that impossible.

shorts.title: Parallel lists
shorts.hook: "Two lists, one for names, one for marks."
shorts.script: Two lists, one for names, one for marks. They match only by position. Sort one list, and the match is gone. Asha gets Ravi's marks, and Python says nothing. Parallel lists are fragile. There is a better way, and it is called a class. Try it in your own file and watch what happens. Pause the video and type it out yourself. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Parallel lists break easily.

shorts.title: What is a class
shorts.script: A class is a blueprint. It describes one type of thing, such as a student, a book or a bank account. Think of a cookie cutter. The cutter is the class. Each cookie you press out is an object. One blueprint, as many objects as you like. Pause the video and type it out yourself. Say it out loud once. Then you remember it. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: A class is a blueprint.

shorts.title: What is an object
shorts.hook: "An object is one real thing made from a class."
shorts.script: An object is one real thing made from a class. Write the class name with brackets, and Python builds one. Student with brackets gives a student. Do it twice, and you get two separate students. Each keeps its own name and its own marks. Say it out loud once. Then you remember it. Then run it, and compare with what you predicted. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: An object is one thing made from a class.

shorts.title: The silent bug
shorts.script: Here is a sneaky bug. You sort the names list, but not the marks list. No error appears. The output simply pairs the wrong name with the wrong marks. Silent bugs are the hardest. Keep each name and its marks in one bundle, and this cannot happen. Then run it, and compare with what you predicted. Try it in your own file and watch what happens. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Silent bugs are the worst.
